title: Vaisakhi, 1699: the call
hook: before a great crowd the Guru draws his sword and asks who will give their head

segments.voice: Yesterday, a court of poets at Anandpur, and a Sufi saint at Bhangani. Your line was pen and sword. Did you balance something hard with something beautiful? Day eighty-four.

Look back at this week. Three companions who did not bend. A Guru who gave his head in Chandni Chowk for another's faith. Two men who carried him home. A boy by the river in Patna. His answer to his father. The court of poets. Everything in the story so far has been building to one morning. It's spring, 1699, at Anandpur. The harvest festival of Vaisakhi. The Guru has sent word across Punjab and beyond: come. And they come, in huge numbers, tens of thousands, tradition says, filling the hillside. They expect hymns, a festival, a blessing. The Guru steps out before them with a drawn sword. Today, the call.
screen: `A WEEK THAT BUILDS TO ONE MORNING.` → `ANANDPUR, SPRING 1699.` → `A DRAWN SWORD.`

segments.voice: Vaisakhi is the spring harvest festival of Punjab, when the wheat is cut, held in the month of Vaisakh, usually around the middle of April. For centuries it was a time of fairs and gatherings. After 1699 it became something more for Sikhs: the birthday of the Khalsa. Here's what happened, as Sikh tradition tells it. The Guru stood before the crowd, sword raised, and asked a question that stopped every heart on the hillside. Is there anyone here who will give me their head? Silence. Nobody moved. He asked again. Then a third time. Finally one man stood up: Daya Ram, a shopkeeper from Lahore. The Guru took him into a tent. There was a sound. The Guru came out alone, with blood on his sword, and asked again: who else will give their head? People began to slip away, frightened. Some went to the Guru's mother to complain he'd lost his mind. And still, a second man stood. Then a third. A fourth. A fifth. Each went into the tent. Each time the Guru came out alone. What happened inside the tent? The sources don't say clearly, and Sikhs tell it in more than one way. Some accounts say the five were never harmed, that the blood was from an animal, or that it was a test of faith all along. The tradition as most Sikhs tell it simply leaves the tent closed. What matters is the question, and the five who answered it. Tomorrow, the tent opens.
screen: `VAISAKHI — THE HARVEST FESTIVAL.` · `WHO WILL GIVE ME THEIR HEAD?` · `DAYA RAM STANDS FIRST.` · `FIVE GO INTO THE TENT.` · then, large: `WHO WILL GIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with what you'd give everything for. Settle and breathe. Let the Guru's question come to you gently, not as a demand, just as a question. What in your life matters so much you'd give everything for it? A person. A value. A faith. A child. You don't need to answer quickly. Let the answer rise, or not. Just sit on the hillside with the question, the way the crowd did, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Vaisakhi. The spring harvest festival of Punjab, and for Sikhs, the day in 1699 when the Guru asked who would give their head.
Your line: who will give. Today, when something needs a volunteer, a task, a hand, a first step, be the one who stands up. Day eighty-four, the end of another week.

howItsDone: Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi each April as the birth of the Khalsa, with gurdwara services, processions called nagar kirtan, and, for many, taking amrit on or near the day.

fork.setup: you're in the crowd at Anandpur. the Guru, sword raised, asks: who will give me their head? what do you do?

go and tell his mother he's lost his mind.
fork.reveal: most of the crowd froze; some left or complained. after the third call, Daya Ram stood up, and four more followed him.

what a scholar hears: Vaisakhi falls in the month of Vaisakh, around April 13 or 14; the 1699 events are known from Sikh tradition and later chronicles.
